papers.title: Reliability of retrospective self-report of shift work exposure in a large occupational cohort
papers.abstract: Objectives: To examine agreement between baseline and retrospective assessments of shift work exposure and test whether this differs in cancer and cardiometabolic disease patients. Methods: A subgroup of the Airwave Health Monitoring study, a cohort of police employees, self-reported shift work status at study entry and retrospectively at follow-up. Agreement statistics were computed overall and stratified by subsequent cancer and cardiometabolic disease status. Adjusted logistic regression tested whether discordant reporting differed by disease status. Results: Overall agreement was 86% (95% CI = 84-88%; {kappa} = 0.72), with no evidence of asymmetric misclassification (McNemar's p = 0.32). Agreement was similar among participants who later developed cancer ({kappa} = 0.76) but lower, although imprecisely estimated, among those who developed cardiometabolic disease ({kappa} = 0.56). Adjusted odds of discordant reporting did not differ significantly by cancer (OR = 0.96, 95% CI= 0.39-2.05) or cardiometabolic disease status (OR = 1.85, 95% CI = 0.81-3.87). Conclusions: Retrospective shift work reports showed good overall reliability, with no evidence of asymmetric misclassification, though reliability varied somewhat by disease outcome. These findings provide an empirical basis for future studies using retrospective shift work exposure in the AHMS and similar cohorts.

papers.title: Prenatal extreme heat exposure and neonatal mortality in Bangladesh, 2015 to 2025: a national birth-history study
papers.abstract: BackgroundHeat in pregnancy is linked to preterm birth and stillbirth, but its link with neonatal death in South Asia is unclear. We estimated this association in Bangladesh and separated the role of prenatal heat from that of the season in which a child is born. MethodsWe included 46,752 live births (February 2015 to May 2025) from the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025 birth history. Each birth was linked to daily maximum temperature from the ERA5 reanalysis at the location of its survey cluster. An extreme heat day was a day on which the maximum temperature reached the clusters 95th percentile of daily maximum temperature for 2014 to 2024. Because gestational age was not recorded, we counted extreme heat days in estimated trimesters, dated back 280 days from birth. Weighted Poisson regression with fixed effects for district, division by calendar month of birth, and year of birth compared births within the same place, season and year. Extreme heat 28 to 55 days after birth, which cannot cause a neonatal death, served as a negative control exposure. ResultsThere were 1,039 neonatal deaths (22.7 per 1,000 live births, 95% CI 21.1 to 24.4). Mortality was highest for births in December to February (26.5 per 1,000, 23.0 to 29.9) and lowest in September to November (17.3, 14.5 to 20.0). Pregnancies had a mean of 13.5 extreme heat days (95% CI 13.4 to 13.6), rising from 4.0 for births in 2018 to 29.5 for births in 2024. The primary estimate was for the estimated third trimester. Per 5 extreme heat days, its adjusted rate ratio was 1.06 (0.98 to 1.15), a risk difference of 1.4 per 1,000 births (-0.6 to 3.3). The rate ratio was 1.04 (0.98 to 1.09) for the whole pregnancy and 0.92 (0.77 to 1.09) for the last 4 weeks of pregnancy. The negative control window showed no clear association (0.92, 0.79 to 1.08). Third trimester estimates were similar with MERRA-2 temperature (1.04, 0.97 to 1.12) and with a fixed 1991 to 2020 threshold (1.07, 1.00 to 1.14). Without control for calendar month of birth, each 1 {degrees}C higher mean third trimester maximum temperature was associated with lower mortality (rate ratio 0.96, 0.93 to 0.99). ConclusionsIn this national birth-history analysis, neonatal mortality varied by season of birth and was highest for births in December to February. When births were compared within the same district, season and year, estimated prenatal extreme heat was not clearly associated with neonatal death. The confidence intervals did not exclude modest increases in risk, and the study had 80% power only for a rate ratio of 1.12 per 5 days or larger. Both gestational age and heat exposure were estimated with error. Studies of prenatal heat and newborn survival should control for season of birth, because season can hide or create an apparent effect of heat.

papers.title: Carbapenem Resistance Among Gram-Negative Bacteria in Bioaerosols at Biomedical Waste Disposal Site in Ahmedabad, India
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global public health concern, with Gram-negative carbapenem-resistant bacteria (CRG) classified by WHO as critical priority pathogens. Biomedical waste disposal sites (BMWs) may act as reservoirs for resistant organisms, posing occupational and community risks. This study investigated the phenotypic and genotypic characterization of Gram-negative carbapenem resistant bacteria in bioaerosols collected from BMW facilities in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India. Bioaerosols were sampled using active Six-stage Andersen Impactors and passive settled plates. Isolates were identified by MALDI-TOF, followed by antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST). Whole genome sequencing (WGS) was performed for 26 representative isolates, and resistance gene profiling was conducted using CARD and ResFinder databases. Representative isolates belonged to Moraxellaceae, Enterobacteriaceae, and Pseudomonadaceae families. All species showed resistance to linezolid, and approximately 60% were multidrug resistant to carbapenems, cephalosporins, and fluoroquinolones. Genotypic analysis confirmed the prevalence of carbapenemase genes, with blaNDM-1 most frequent, followed by blaNDM-7, blaVIM-2, blaVIM-11, blaOXA-23, and blaOXA-235. This is the first report documenting Acinetobacter baumannii, A. schindleri, A. towneri, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas juntendi in bioaerosols from BMW sites. Biomedical waste environments serve as critical reservoirs of AMR. These findings emphasize the need for surveillance, protective measures, and integration of environmental AMR monitoring into public health policy.

papers.title: Community-Level Wastewater Surveillance of Nicotine Biomarkers Tracks Cardiovascular Disease Burden and Myocardial Infarction
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDTobacco smoking is the largest modifiable contributor to cardiovascular disease (CVD), yet population-level surveillance still relies on self-reported and retail data, which are subject to measuring bias and lag. Urinary and salivary cotinine quantify individual tobacco exposure, but no analogous, objective metric exists at the community level. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) has transformed surveillance of infectious diseases and illicit drug use; whether the same approach can yield a community-level signal of CVD risk is unknown. OBJECTIVEThe primary objective of this study is to track community-level wastewater nicotine biomarkers and evaluate potential correlations with relative CVD burden in El Paso, Texas. METHODSWe integrated wastewater nicotine biomarker surveillance with electronic health record (EHR) data across four sewersheds in El Paso, Texas. Twenty-four-hour composite influent samples were collected monthly (June 2024-May 2025; n=48) and quantified by liquid-chromatography tandem mass spectrometry for five nicotine metabolites. Cotinine, nornicotine, and trans-3-hydroxycotinine (3HC) were detected in 91.6-100% of samples, whereas tobacco-specific nitrosamines were below limit of detection. CVD cases (January 2021-December 2024) were obtained from the Paso del Norte Health Information Exchange and mapped to sewersheds by residential ZIP code using ArcGIS. At the sewershed level, population-normalized nicotine mass loads tracked the proportional burden of atherosclerosis/ischemia/infarction and heart failure. Across the sewersheds, monthly 3HC mass load and the nicotine metabolite ratio (NMR) were strongly and specifically associated with incident ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) (3HC vs. STEMI:{rho} = 0.893, p = 0.012), without parallel associations for non-ST-elevation or old myocardial infarction. CONCLUSIONSTo our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that integrating wastewater nicotine surveillance with EHR data can reveal community-level 3HC and NMR as specific indicators of incident STEMI. Our findings indicate wastewater surveillance as a novel, objective tool to inform cessation policy and CVD prevention. Lay WordsO_LIThis study investigated using wastewater to measure population-level nicotine consumption and to see if it was related to local cardiovascular disease. C_LIO_LIThe study took place in El Paso, Texas, USA across 4 different wastewater treatment collection points over the course of one year. C_LIO_LIThree metabolites of human nicotine consumption were detected in wastewater samples. The increased nicotine mass loads were proportional with community-level heart failure and atherosclerosis. C_LIO_LIWastewater can be a helpful tool to inform cardiovascular disease prevention efforts and smoking cessation practices. C_LI

papers.title: Brick kilns, child respiratory symptoms and blood lead in Bangladesh: a national geospatial analysis of the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey
papers.abstract: BackgroundBrick kilns are a major source of air pollution in Bangladesh. Their effects on child respiratory health and lead exposure have not been studied nationally with blood measures. MethodsWe linked a 2018 to 2019 satellite map of 6,978 kilns to the 3,149 displaced clusters of the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025. Exposure was the number of kilns within 5 km. Outcomes were cough and acute respiratory infection (ARI) symptoms in 23,357 children under 5 years, and venous blood lead in 10,622 children aged 12 to 59 months. We fitted survey-weighted modified Poisson models with district fixed effects. Diarrhoea and interview timing relative to the firing season served as negative controls. FindingsThree in four children (75.4%, 95% CI 73.6 to 77.1) lived within 5 km of a kiln, and 20.3% (18.7 to 22.0) had ten or more. Exposure rose with wealth. Compared with no kiln, ten or more kilns were not associated with cough (adjusted prevalence ratio [PR] 1.05, 0.96 to 1.16), ARI symptoms (1.21, 0.90 to 1.62) or blood lead of 5 {micro}g/dL or more (0.94, 0.85 to 1.03; crude PR 1.27, 1.14 to 1.41). Per 10 kilns, the ARI PR was 1.11 (1.01 to 1.21), but a spline showed no association (P=0.153). Cough was not associated with kiln density at the peak of firing (PR per 10 kilns 1.00, 0.96 to 1.05) but was in May and June (1.10, 1.04 to 1.17). The lead result held in all sensitivity analyses. InterpretationAt survey resolution, living among more kilns was not linked to blood lead. Weak respiratory associations, absent at peak firing, fit confounding by place better than an acute effect of kiln smoke. Studies with exact locations should measure effects within 1 to 2 km of kilns. FundingNone.

papers.title: Working from home a few times a month to a few times a week is associated with higher psychological distress: between- and within-person analyses of a five-wave panel of employees in Japan
papers.abstract: PurposeTo estimate the association between the frequency of working from home (WFH) and psychological distress among employees in Japan, separating between-person from within-person differences, and to examine this association by sex and household circumstances. MethodsWe used five annual waves (2021-2025) of the nationwide Japan COVID-19 and Society Internet Survey (JACSIS), including 39,773 employees aged [≥]18 years who worked in the past month (78,498 person-waves). The exposure was the frequency of WFH in the past month (seven categories). The outcomes were the Kessler 6 (K6) score (0-24), K6 [≥]5, and K6 [≥]13. We used within-between linear regression, overall and by sex and household circumstances at the first wave. ResultsCompared with no WFH, WFH 2-3 times a month, once a week, and 2-3 times a week was associated with K6 scores higher by 1.99, 1.80, and 0.67 points between persons and by 0.53 (95% CI 0.28, 0.77), 0.45 (0.20, 0.69), and 0.35 (0.10, 0.60) points within persons, and with a 3.5-4.6 percentage point higher probability of K6 [≥]5 within persons. These within-person K6 differences were positive in all sex and household groups (0.20-0.63 points) but imprecise. For the other frequencies, the within-person differences were 0.03-0.20 points. ConclusionWFH 2-3 times a month or once a week, and also 2-3 times a week, was associated with higher psychological distress, both between and within persons. Support for employees who sometimes work from home should consider the frequency of WFH together with their work and family situations.

papers.title: Multimorbidity and cardiometabolic clustering among university employees: findings from a comprehensive health assessment program in India
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo estimate the burden and patterns of multimorbidity and cardiometabolic multimorbidity among university employees undergoing a comprehensive health assessment programme, and to examine demographic and behavioural factors associated with multimorbidity. DesignCross-sectional study. SettingA public university in Maharashtra, India. ParticipantsA total of 266 university employees who underwent a comprehensive health assessment were included. Main outcome measuresMultimorbidity was defined as the presence of two or more of nine chronic conditions: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, ischaemic heart disease, chronic kidney disease, thyroid disease, stroke, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cancer. Cardiometabolic multimorbidity was defined as the presence of two or more of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, ischaemic heart disease and chronic kidney disease. ResultsHypertension was identified in 119 participants (44.7%), comprising 50 participants with pre-existing hypertension and 69 newly identified during the assessment. Dyslipidaemia was present in 189 (71.1%) and diabetes mellitus in 45 (16.9%). Overall, 108 participants (40.6%) had multimorbidity and 103 (38.7%) had cardiometabolic multimorbidity. The prevalence of multimorbidity increased progressively with age, from 17.5% among participants aged <30 years to 83.3% among those aged [≥]60 years. The predominant exact multimorbidity patterns were hypertension with dyslipidaemia alone (49 participants) and hypertension, diabetes mellitus and dyslipidaemia (27 participants). Overall, 173 participants (65.0%) had at least one newly identified hypertension, diabetes mellitus or dyslipidaemia diagnosis. In multivariable logistic regression, age (adjusted OR [aOR] 1.058 per year, 95% CI 1.027 to 1.091), BMI (aOR 1.163 per kg/m2, 95% CI 1.076 to 1.257) and tobacco use (aOR 3.296, 95% CI 1.377 to 7.888) were independently associated with multimorbidity. The model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.731. ConclusionMultimorbidity affected approximately two in five university employees, with cardiometabolic conditions accounting for most of the observed disease clustering. Comprehensive health assessment identified a substantial burden of previously unrecognised chronic disease. Integrating institutional or occupational health assessment with longitudinal primary care follow-up may provide an opportunity for earlier detection, risk-factor modification and coordinated management of multimorbidity.

papers.title: Occupational burnout in the UK film and television industry: A cross-sectional survey of mental health, job quality, perceived stigma, and sexual harassment
papers.abstract: Recent industry surveys have reported widespread concern about mental health, working conditions, and harassment in the UK film and television industry, but no peer-reviewed empirical study has examined the determinants of occupational burnout in this workforce. The present study tested whether physical health, mental wellbeing, perceived public stigma, intrinsic job quality, and sexual harassment exposure predict burnout in industry professionals. A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 415 individuals across more than 100 job titles, with 286 also completing an optional harassment module. Mental wellbeing sat well below population norms, with 68% scoring in the range indicative of probable depressive symptoms and 82% in the high-exhaustion range on the Maslach Burnout Inventory General Survey. Mental wellbeing and intrinsic job quality were the strongest predictors of burnout (R{superscript 2} = .56), with meaningfulness accounting for most of the job-quality effect. Working hours independently predicted emotional exhaustion. Harassment exposure was associated with burnout in women but not men, approximately 30% mediated by mental wellbeing; sexist behaviour directly predicted exhaustion in women. Workers with a disability reported higher stigma. Burnout was strongly associated with intent to leave, and the findings collectively indicate an industry-wide occupational health concern requiring structural rather than individual-level intervention.

papers.title: Change in the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio after a 3-day orbital flight: A preregistered secondary analysis of NASA open data from the Inspiration4 civilian crew
papers.abstract: BackgroundCommercial spaceflight now carries civilians on short missions, yet their stress-axis physiology is poorly described. Earlier shuttle data suggest that sympathetic responses predominate after short flights and glucocorticoid responses after long ones. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) is a low-cost readout of both. MethodsPreregistered secondary analysis of open clinical laboratory data (NASA Open Science Data Repository OSD-569 and OSD-575) from the four Inspiration4 crew members, each sampled seven times: three draws before launch, one the day after return (R+1) and three during recovery (R+45 to R+194). Log-transformed NLR was modelled with a linear mixed model with a random intercept per crew member and Kenward-Roger inference. Lymphocyte and eosinophil counts and C-reactive protein were secondary outcomes with false discovery rate correction. ResultsAll 28 draws were analysed. NLR at R+1 did not differ from pre-flight (fold change 1.04; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.34; p = 0.73); two crew members increased (+25% and +46%) and two decreased (-27% and-11%). During recovery NLR was 23% lower than pre-flight (fold change 0.77; 95% CI 0.64 to 0.92; p = 0.005). No secondary outcome changed after correction; lymphocytes were 18% lower at R+1 (95% CI -35% to +4%; q = 0.31). Between-person differences explained 58% of the variance. An ordinary regression ignoring repeated measures missed the recovery effect (p = 0.08). ConclusionsA 3-day orbital flight produced no consistent leukocyte stress signature one day after return. The lower NLR during recovery suggests that pre-flight values, not recovery values, deviate from the resting state, which has implications for how baselines are defined in short-duration spaceflight studies.

papers.title: Wildfire smoke leaves a large five-year imprint on mortality in the United States
papers.abstract: Wildfire smoke poses a growing health risk worldwide, yet the magnitude and temporal evolution of mortality after episodic exposure remain poorly resolved, limiting burden assessment. Using monthly county-level wildfire PM2.5 and mortality data from the United State, we exploit episodic exposure contrasts to deconvolve overlapping mortality responses and recover the impulse-response function. The excess mortality response peaks approximately three years after an exposure pulse and subsides by five years. We estimate 1.7 (95% uncertainty interval: 1.1-2.3) million smoke-associated deaths during 2011-2023, approximately ten times estimates using long-term ambient PM2.5 mortality relative risks. Circulatory and respiratory diseases contribute comparably and dominate this burden. Responses are markedly greater among adults [≥]65 years; during the COVID-19 pandemic, population-wide cumulative responses are significantly higher over at least the first seven months after exposure. Reducing wildfire smoke exposure can thus yield substantial health benefits over multiple years, particularly when population vulnerability is heightened.

papers.title: Professional Identity and Its Influencing Factors Among Nursing Interns: The Mediating Role of Career Adaptability Between Social Support and Professional Identity
papers.abstract: PurposeThe internship period is a critical stage for nursing students to develop professional values. This study aimed to investigate the current status of professional identity among nursing interns, analyze the effects of social support, perceived stress, psychological resilience, and career adaptability on professional identity, and explore the mediating role of career adaptability between social support and professional identity, so as to provide empirical evidence for enhancing professional identity and optimizing nursing talent training systems. MethodsUsing convenience sampling, 407 nursing interns from a tertiary hospital in Quanzhou were selected as participants from May to July 2025. Data were collected using a general information questionnaire, the Social Support Scale, the Perceived Stress Scale, the Psychological Resilience Scale, the Professional Identity Questionnaire for Nursing Students, the Career Adaptability Scale, and the Questionnaire for Nurse Intention to Retention Employed. SPSS 26.0 was used for reliability analysis, descriptive analysis, independent samples t-test, one-way ANOVA, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression analysis. The PROCESS macro was employed to test the mediating effect. ResultsThe total score of professional identity among nursing interns was (61.74{+/-}11.08), with 73.5% showing moderate professional identity. Parents attitude toward nursing, reasons for choosing the profession, personal attitude toward the major, and employment intention showed statistically significant differences in professional identity scores (p<0.05). Pearson correlation analysis revealed that professional identity was significantly positively correlated with social support (r=0.474), psychological resilience (r=0.389), and career adaptability (r=0.609) (p<0.01), and significantly negatively correlated with perceived stress (r=-0.378) (p<0.01). Multiple linear regression analysis indicated that career adaptability ({beta}=0.309, p<0.001) and social support ({beta}=0.383, p<0.001) were significant positive predictors of professional identity, whereas reasons for choosing the profession ({beta}=-3.603, p=0.001) and employment intention ({beta}=-7.116, p<0.001) were significant negative predictors. The model explained 49.2% of the variance in professional identity. Mediation effect analysis showed that career adaptability played a partial mediating role between social support and professional identity, with a mediation effect value of 0.288 (95% CI: 0.221-0.363), accounting for 40.2% of the total effect. ConclusionsNursing interns professional identity is at a moderately high level. Social support and career adaptability are positive influencing factors. Career adaptability plays a partial mediating role between social support and professional identity; social support indirectly enhances professional identity by strengthening career adaptability.

papers.title: Peak Agricultural Pesticide Spray Seasons Are Associated with worse Negative Affect and Behavioral Dysregulation in Adolescents and Young Adults: A 2-Year Ecological Momentary Assessment Study in ESPINA
papers.abstract: IntroductionPesticide exposure has been associated with poorer mental health, yet little is known about whether seasonal fluctuations in agricultural pesticide use are associated with cyclical changes in mood. We evaluated associations between 10 peak and off-peak pesticide spray seasons and ecological momentary assessment (EMA)-derived mood in a floricultural region in Ecuador. Methods496 adolescent and young adult participants completed repeated EMAs over 2.5 years, including one single-assessment administration and nine 10-day bursts (Nassessments=14,332). Mood outcomes included negative affect (sadness, anxiety, stress, anger; overall mean [SD]=2.79 [1.32]), positive affect (happiness, motivation; mean=4.21 [1.60]), behavioral dysregulation (aggression and impulsivity; mean=1.86 [1.29]), and fatigue and concentration (tiredness and difficulty concentrating; mean=3.25 [1.34]). Generalized linear mixed models estimated pooled, between-person and within-person associations between peak pesticide spray seasons and mood, adjusting for demographic and longitudinal factors. Effect modification by sex, floricultural occupation, and cohabitation with a floricultural worker was assessed. ResultsPeak spray seasons were associated with higher negative affect ({beta}=0.11 [0.06, 0.16]) and behavioral dysregulation ({beta}=0.10 [0.05, 0.15]), fatigue and difficulty concentrating ({beta}=0.06 [0.001, 0.12]), but not positive affect ({beta}=0.01 [-0.05, 0.07]), Associations were driven by within-person changes. Sex modified associations with anger, which were stronger in males than females. Floricultural occupation modified associations, with greater behavioral dysregulation and lower positive affect among floricultural workers than non-workers. DiscussionPeak pesticide spray seasons were associated with worsening negative affect, behavioral dysregulation, and fatigue and concentration. EMA may provide a sensitive approach for detecting short-term neurobehavioral changes associated with seasonal pesticide exposure.

papers.title: Serum PFOS Concentration and Isomer Composition in Relation to Depressive Symptoms in Young Adults
papers.abstract: Total serum perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) concentration and its isomer composition describe different aspects of internal exposure, but their respective associations with depressive symptoms remain uncertain. We examined adults aged 18-25 years in NHANES August 2021-August 2023 using survey-weighted models of the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Total measured PFOS was the sum of linear PFOS and pooled monomethyl-branched PFOS; composition was their log-ratio. The analytic cohort included 169 participants, with 147 complete cases for core adjustment. Median total PFOS was 1.70 ng/mL, the median linear fraction was 72.2%, and the weighted prevalence of PHQ-9 [≥]10 was 22.6%. In the joint adjusted model, a doubling of total PFOS at fixed composition corresponded to -0.49 PHQ-9 points (95% CI, -1.65 to 0.68); a doubling of the linear-to-branched ratio at fixed total corresponded to 0.21 points (-1.94 to 2.36). Algebraic rescaling across the reported interquartile ranges yielded differences of -0.58 points (-1.95 to 0.81) for total PFOS and 0.13 points (-1.16 to 1.41) for composition. The inverse continuous-score association weakened with adjustment, whereas the screening odds ratio primarily lost precision. Excluding three observations with an isomer below detection shifted both joint coefficients. The data therefore do not establish an independent composition association or equivalent isomer effects. Experimental evidence supports candidate oxidative, inflammatory, and synaptic pathways, but differential protein binding and elimination prevent a serum composition ratio from being interpreted directly as brain dose or toxicity. Larger longitudinal analyses with isomer-resolved exposure and toxicokinetic measurements are needed to test these pathways.

papers.title: Cardiovascular Risk Stratification Among University Employees in India: Comparison of WHO/ISH, ASCVD and Framingham Risk Models
papers.abstract: BackgroundCardiovascular disease (CVD) risk prediction is an important component of primary prevention, particularly in populations with increasing cardiometabolic risk. Several risk prediction models are available, but their estimates may differ because of differences in derivation populations, predictors, calibration, and cardiovascular outcomes. Evidence comparing these models within Indian occupational populations remains limited. This study compared 10-year CVD risk estimates generated by the World Health Organization/International Society of Hypertension (WHO/ISH) cardiovascular risk charts, the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) Pooled Cohort Equation (ASCVD-PCE), and the Framingham general cardiovascular disease risk equation among university employees in India. MethodsA comparative observational study was conducted using standardized health assessment data from 266 university employees. Participants aged 40-74 years were selected to provide a common analytical age range across the three risk prediction approaches. Of 127 employees within this age range, three with documented previous ischemic heart disease were excluded because the analysis focused on primary prevention. The final analytical cohort comprised 124 participants. Blood pressure was assessed using a standardized protocol involving three readings at five-minute intervals, with repeat assessments during three subsequent weekly visits for employees with elevated initial readings. Ten-year cardiovascular risk was estimated using the 2019 WHO/ISH laboratory-based risk charts for the South Asian region, the ASCVD-PCE, and the 2008 Framingham general CVD equation. Agreement between risk categories was assessed using Cohens kappa and linear weighted kappa. Agreement was also examined at [≥]10% and [≥]20% thresholds. ResultsThe mean age of the 124 participants was 47.63 {+/-} 6.45 years, and 86.3% were male. Diabetes was present in 25.8%, smoking/tobacco use in 19.4%, and 29.0% were receiving antihypertensive treatment. Mean estimated risk was 5.94% for WHO/ISH, 5.95% for ASCVD-PCE, and 12.86% for Framingham. High risk ([≥]20%) was identified in 2.4%, 4.8%, and 20.2% of participants by WHO/ISH, ASCVD-PCE, and Framingham, respectively. Exact four-category agreement was 70.2% between WHO/ISH and ASCVD-PCE, compared with 31.5% between WHO/ISH and Framingham and 26.6% between ASCVD-PCE and Framingham. Cohens kappa was 0.502 for WHO/ISH versus ASCVD-PCE, 0.079 for WHO/ISH versus Framingham, and 0.047 for ASCVD-PCE versus Framingham. Weighted kappa values were 0.639, 0.323, and 0.342, respectively. ConclusionWHO/ISH and ASCVD-PCE produced closely similar mean risk estimates and substantially greater categorical agreement than either model showed with the Framingham equation. Framingham generated considerably higher 10-year CVD risk estimates and classified a larger proportion of participants into higher-risk categories. These findings highlight the importance of model selection when cardiovascular risk assessment is undertaken in Indian occupational populations and support cautious interpretation of risk estimates derived from models developed in different populations and for different cardiovascular endpoints.

papers.title: Estimating excess mortality during heat waves using a causal inference framework and non-randomized time series
papers.abstract: Researchers must often rely on observational data to draw conclusions about the causal relationship between an exposure and an outcome. This is common in environmental epidemiology research, where the assignment to an exposure can be unethical or impossible. Consider a setting in which we seek to estimate excess mortality during heat waves, but are unable to randomize individuals to moderate or extreme heat. We propose to follow a causal framework for non-randomized time series that uses what we call historical time series matching to construct hypothetical randomized experiments, in which background covariates are balanced. We applied this framework and assessed the following causal question: Are daily mortality counts among elderly Americans higher during hot versus warm summer time periods? We addressed this causal question by drawing frequentist, Fisherian, and Bayesian inferences for five American cities. We estimated the average treatment effect of heat on three-day mortality with 95% Fisherian intervals to be 0.5 [-3.6, 4.4] deaths in Pittsburgh, 3.7 [0.7, 6.6] deaths in Seattle, 12.5 [6.1, 18.9] deaths in Chicago, 8.5 [1.4, 15.6] deaths in Los Angeles, and 20.3 [11.2, 29.5] deaths in New York.

papers.title: Predicting Air Conditioner Ownership in Low- and Middle-Income Countries using Geospatial Machine Learning Methods - Mapping Cooling Inequality
papers.abstract: BackgroundRising global temperatures are intensifying exposure to extreme heat, yet access to air conditioning (AC) remains unequal which leaves vulnerable populations without protection against the heat. Household survey data on AC ownership is scarce in low- and middle-income countries limiting the ability to identify areas of cooling gaps. MethodsIn this study, we develop a geospatial machine learning framework that integrates household data from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) program with high resolution climatic, socioeconomic and demographic covariates to generate a 5km resolution prediction of AC ownership across low- and middle-income countries in Africa and Asia for the year 2023. ResultsThe resulting map reveals strong spatial inequalities with high predicted prevalence in wealthier and urban regions, and near zero prevalence across much of Central and West Africa and rural areas. These patterns reflect the adaptation cooling gap where those most exposed to extreme heat are least able to adapt through access to cooling. ConclusionBy producing the first continental-scale, high resolution map of AC ownership, this study lays the foundation for designing and targeting equitable cooling strategies, support heat-health planning particularly in communities most affected and informing sustainable energy policy.

papers.title: Inhalation exposure to methamphetamine in contaminated residences
papers.abstract: Current health risk assessments from thirdhand exposure to methamphetamine (meth) to occupants of contaminated residences when no cooking or use is still occurring assume that inhalation exposure is insignificant. After Wright et al. (2021) reported substantial meth concentrations in a contaminated residence, the present study was conducted to further test the hypothesis that concentrations were high enough to contribute to total occupant dose. Air sampling was conducted in contaminated residences that had been previously sampled for surface contamination. Samples were collected on personal sampling pumps in fixed locations on treated glass fiber filters is cassettes and analyzed by gas or liquid chromatography with mass spectroscopy. Sixty-nine samples were collected from eighteen residences for the study. Meth concentrations ranged from 0.02 to 15 g/m3. Concentrations in supply air vents were significantly higher than in return vents or in ambient air. Residences with no HVAC systems (baseboard heat) had airborne concentrations similar to residences with HVAC systems turned off, and lower than when HVAC was on. Whether a residence was occupied or not did not show differences. All data from residences with HVAC had a significant correlation with surface concentrations (R2 = 0.61) but some factors that affected results were not determined in the study. In the context of the risk assessment and regulatory standard established by California and adopted in several other states, the inhalation exposure would approximately double total occupant dose for infants, and this population would exceed the California reference dose by approximately 100%. Further studies should be conducted to refine these estimates and determine the factors that influence airborne concentrations.

papers.title: Source-water salinity measured by electrical conductivity in Bangladesh, 2025: a nationally representative cross-sectional survey
papers.abstract: BackgroundIn coastal Bangladesh, saline drinking water has been linked to raised blood pressure. The 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) measured electrical conductivity (EC), a salinity indicator, in source water, but its report gave no population counts or district estimates. ObjectivesTo estimate how many people live in households whose tested source has high EC, and to describe patterns by place, household characteristics, source type and arsenic. MethodsEC was measured in source water of 6,040 households in 64 districts, February to June. In 14.5% of households the tested source was not the main drinking-water source. Primary outcomes were EC above 1,500 and 3,000 {micro}S/cm, survey risk classes that are not health-based standards. Estimates were survey weighted; comparisons were observational. ResultsEC exceeded 1,500 {micro}S/cm in 5.3% of households (95% CI 4.7 to 5.9), about 9.0 million people, including 1.8 million above 3,000 {micro}S/cm. Coastal-zone districts held 26% of households but 70% of those above 1,500 {micro}S/cm. Shares varied little by wealth or in households with young children or pregnant women. Nationally, deep tube wells more often had high EC because most are coastal. In the coastal zone, deep and shallow wells had similar shares (16.1% and 17.9%). After district adjustment, EC was about 18% lower in deep wells (geometric mean ratio 0.82, 0.73 to 0.92). Within upazilas (restricted sample) it was 0.93 (0.80 to 1.07). Arsenic above 10 ppb was more common where EC was high, but this link weakened after district adjustment. ConclusionsMillions of people live in households whose tested source has high EC, mostly in coastal and south-central districts. Deep wells had modestly lower EC after geographic adjustment, but the difference shrank within upazilas and depended on the handling of implausibly low readings. The findings support measuring EC alongside arsenic, with documented meter calibration.

papers.title: Ambient temperature and impacts on preterm birth: A storyline approach
papers.abstract: BackgroundNon-optimal air temperature increases the risk of preterm birth, but how temperature-related risks may translate into future population burden remains uncertain. We aimed to estimate the association between temperature and preterm birth in Sweden and assess how preterm birth burden may change under plausible future temperature conditions. MethodsWe conducted a nationwide population-based cohort study of singleton births in Sweden from 1973 to 2018. Weekly mean temperature was assigned at the parish level according to maternal residence. Cox proportional hazards models with a distributed lag nonlinear model were used to estimate nonlinear and delayed associations between temperature and preterm birth. The estimated exposure-response relationship and baseline hazards were then incorporated into an individual-based microsimulation of gestational progression under projected temperatures for 2025-2055. Future projections were examined across multiple climate models under SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0 scenarios. Outcomes included the annual number and cumulative incidence of preterm births and the temperature-attributable fraction. ResultsAmong 4,338,825 singleton births, 211,397 (4.9%) were preterm. Temperature-preterm birth associations were modest overall. The clearest increase in hazard was observed following exposure to very low temperatures, particularly -10{degrees}C at short lags. Higher temperatures showed no clear increase in risk. From 2025 to 2055, the annual cumulative incidence of preterm birth and the temperature-attributable fraction was expected to remain broadly stable, with limited differences between emissions scenarios. In contrast, the absolute number of preterm births was expected to over the projection period, primarily reflecting increases in the projected number of pregnancies rather than substantial changes in temperature-associated risk. ConclusionsVery low temperatures were associated with a modest short-term increase in preterm birth risk in Sweden, hot temperatures showed little evidence of increased risk. Applying these associations to future climate conditions suggested limited changes in preterm birth incidence or the proportion attributable to temperature through 2055. However, the absolute burden of preterm birth may increase as the population at risk grows. This highlights the importance of considering demographic change alongside climate projections when assessing future maternal and neonatal health burden.

papers.title: Arsenic in drinking-water sources in Bangladesh, 2012-13 to 2025: national trends, geographic persistence and implications for well testing
papers.abstract: BackgroundChronic arsenic exposure in drinking water causes skin lesions and cancers and raises infant, cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in Bangladesh. National surveys tested source water in 2012-13, 2019 and 2025 with different kits, so the trend is uncertain. ObjectivesWe estimated how arsenic in source water changed after laboratory adjustment of 2012-13 readings, and how many people remained exposed. We also assessed whether districts high in earlier surveys held most people exposed in 2025. MethodsWe analysed 11,624 households in three Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys. We counted arsenic strictly above 10 and 50 parts per billion (ppb). Survey-weighted Poisson regression compared rounds, after adjusting 2012-13 readings with the surveys laboratory cross-check. ResultsEstimates reproduced published 2019 and 2025 tables. After laboratory adjustment of 2012-13, the share above 10 ppb fell from 24.0% to 14.4% (adjusted ratio 0.61, sampling 95% CI 0.55 to 0.67; 0.69 with interview month). Above 50 ppb it fell from 10.9% to 8.6% (0.80, 0.69 to 0.93; 0.93 with month). Most of the fall at 10 ppb occurred within source types. Assuming no false positives, the fall would vanish only if later kits detected 61% of sources above 10 ppb. About 26 million people used such water in 2025 (kit scenarios 23 to 32 million). The 25 districts high in 2012-13 and 2019 held 39% of the population but 72% of those exposed (95% CI 68 to 76). Clustering was evident, but no district was a significant hotspot. ConclusionsArsenic above 10 ppb was lower in 2025 than in 2012-13, but the size of the fall depends on unverified later kits. Change at 50 ppb and since 2019 was unclear after month adjustment. One household in seven exceeded the WHO guideline in 2025. Districts found high earlier held most exposed people, supporting prioritised well testing there alongside broader surveillance. Future surveys need one kit with a laboratory cross-check.

papers.title: PFAS Profiles in Private Wells Reveal Septic System Sources of Contamination in a Rural Maine Community
papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are present throughout the environment due to decades of use in many commercial products and industrial processes. These molecules contain a hydrophobic fluorocarbon tail and a functional headgroup (typically a carboxylic or sulfonic acid) that allows hydrophilic interactions with the surrounding environment. These properties make them inherently resistant to degradation, difficult to track through the environment, readily bioaccumulative, and likely to impact human health. Through collaboration with town officials, multiple meetings with local sustainability committee members and school officials, and direct contact with individual homeowners, we conducted community-driven sampling of PFAS in well water from 105 houses in Tremont, ME, a rural coastal town that relies on private wells for drinking water. The rate of PFAS detection for one or more analytes across all wells (N=105) was 69%. Of all wells tested, 16 (15%) exceeded the current public drinking water standard in Maine (20 ng/L for 6 PFAS), and an additional 17 (totaling 31% of all wells tested) exceeded Maines newly adopted public drinking water standards for the state (based on EPA 2024 standards). Because private wells are unregulated, homeowners may use these results as a guide for taking action to maintain safe drinking water. Both hierarchical cluster analyses and pairwise Spearmans rank correlation of PFAS test results revealed similar profiles in households near and far from one another. Along with the absence of obvious, large-scale potential point sources of PFAS contamination, these findings support septic systems as the primary source of PFAS contamination in drinking water across this town. The community-driven approach to the sampling effort has enabled information sharing on the importance of water filtration options, discussion of long-term pollution abatement strategies for individual households and the town, and focused efforts for future well water testing and PFAS mitigation. papers.title: Knowledge and practices toward occupational health and environmental sustainability among farmers in Pabna District, Bangladesh: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Bangladeshs agricultural sector remains heavily dependent on pesticides and chemical inputs, yet limited attention has been paid to how farmers knowledge of occupational health and environmental sustainability translates into actual practice across the full agricultural value chain. This study aimed to assess the knowledge and practices of farmers in Pabna District, Bangladesh, regarding occupational health, pesticide handling, environmentally sustainable farming, and market sanitation. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 301 farmers in 2024 using a structured questionnaire covering socio-demographic characteristics, sustainable farming knowledge and adoption, soil testing and organic farming practices, pesticide handling and occupational health and safety behaviours, post-harvest waste management, and market sanitation conditions. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics. The majority of respondents were male (87.04%) and had no formal education (63.46%). Although most farmers reported knowledge of environmentally sustainable farming practices (97.70%) and pesticide label instructions (98.00%), corresponding safety practices were poor: only 10.63% reported wearing any personal protective equipment and 1.33% reported using a mask during pesticide application. Eye irritation was the most commonly self-reported health symptom following pesticide exposure (92.69%). Market sanitation infrastructure was similarly inadequate, with 89.00% of respondents reporting an absence of sanitary toilets. These findings indicate a consistent gap between farmers knowledge and their actual practices across multiple domains of the agri-food system. Strengthening extension services, delivering practical hands-on occupational safety training, and investing in market sanitation infrastructure are recommended to close this gap and support safer, more sustainable farming practices in Bangladesh.

papers.title: Cross-validation of wearable light loggers across electric and natural light conditions: focus on illuminance, melanopic EDI, and CCT
papers.abstract: Wearable light loggers are increasingly used to assess light exposure in everyday environments in studies of circadian physiology and sleep, yet their accuracy under diverse lighting conditions remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluated three commonly used wearable light loggers (ActLumus, Lido and OcuWEAR) by comparing measurements of photopic illuminance, melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (m-EDI), and correlated colour temperature (CCT) against a reference spectroradiometer under controlled laboratory conditions and in the field. Measurements were conducted across fluorescent, incandescent, and multiple LED sources, as well as under dynamic daylight exposure. Device performance depended strongly on both light source characteristics and metric type. Illuminance exhibited lower variability, whereas m-EDI and CCT showed substantial device- and condition-specific biases, particularly under spectrally atypical illumination conditions. These differences were consistent with spectral mismatch effects arising from standard photometric calibration practices. Importantly, the impact of measurement bias varied by exposure context: under dim light conditions, small absolute deviations led to substantial misclassification relative to currently recommended thresholds, whereas brighter electric light and daylight conditions were more robust. These findings highlight that device- and context-dependent biases can influence the interpretation of light exposure in circadian and sleep research, underscoring the need for careful device selection and data interpretation.

papers.title: No evidence for large causal effects of six air pollutants on non-suppurative otitis media: a two-sample Mendelian randomization study
papers.abstract: BackgroundObservational studies have linked air pollution to otitis media, but confounding and reverse causation preclude causal inference. We used two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) to assess genetic causal effects of six air pollutants on non-suppurative otitis media, represented by otitis media with effusion (OME). MethodsExposure GWAS for PM2.5, PM2.5 absorbance, PM2.5-10, PM10, NO2 and NOx were obtained from UK Biobank (MRC-IEU), and the outcome was FinnGen R13 H8_NONSUPPNAS (12,397 cases, 464,237 controls). Inverse-variance weighting was primary, with MR-Egger, weighted median and mode, MR-PRESSO, leave-one-out and Steiger analyses, reverse MR and exploratory multivariable MR (MVMR). Asthma, allergic rhinitis and chronic rhinosinusitis served as positive controls, and three suppurative otitis media phenotypes served as negative controls. ResultsAfter false-discovery-rate correction, none of the six pollutants was significantly associated with OME; the sole nominal signal was PM10 (OR=1.555, 95% CI 0.947-2.553, P=0.081), which reversed with the 88-SNP pooled set (OR=0.64, 0.24-1.69, P=0.365). At 80% power, minimum detectable ORs ranged widely from 1.69 to 32.09; only PM2.5-10 and PM10 had values near 2, so moderate effects (OR 1.2-1.5) cannot be excluded. Confirmatory positive controls using phenotype-specific instruments were strongly positive, whereas negative-control outcomes showed no associations (all FDR>0.85). Every nominal reverse-MR signal had a significant MR-Egger intercept (the PM2.5 absorbance signal also showed significant heterogeneity and MR-PRESSO tests), indicating horizontal pleiotropy rather than reverse causation. MVMR was exploratory only, as conditional F statistics were below 10. ConclusionsWe found no evidence for large-effect genetic causal associations between the six air pollutants and OME. These null findings argue against large, lifetime-average causal effects, and the associations reported in observational studies may instead reflect residual confounding, shared comorbidity or differences in exposure windows.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Heterogeneity in Heat-Related Health Impacts Across Germany Districts.
papers.abstract: BackgroundMultiple factors can drive heat susceptibility, but are typically analyzed individually. This study investigates high-dimensional heterogeneity across multiple domains in the effect of hot days on emergency hospitalizations across German districts. MethodsWe obtained emergency hospitalization rates per 1,000 in 3-day windows for the summers of 2005-2023 from the German Diagnosis-Related Groups-Statistic, linked with spatio-temporal temperature information. A hot day was defined as at least one day above the district-level 98th percentile heat index. Multiple characteristics of the demographic, health/social, and environmental domains were selected as potential effect modifiers. We implemented a generalized random forest, where outcome and propensity scores were modeled with fixed effects estimators to control for seasonality and district-level confounding. We divided the conditional average treatment effects (CATE) into quartiles to map their spatial distribution and identify key effect modifiers via the variable importance and observed indicator profiles across quartiles. ResultsWe found substantial variation across districts regarding heat-related emergency hospitalizations. The top three indicators for predicting this effect heterogeneity were the percentage of people seeking protection, population below age 6, and air pollution levels. The observed indicator profile for the most susceptible districts was characterized by a larger percentage of vulnerable populations, higher car density, and fewer hospital beds. ConclusionThere is substantial variation in heat susceptibility across and within districts in Germany. We propose an approach that can help understanding such complex interplay of indicators from different domains driving heterogeneity. Research in ContextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe screened PubMed and Web of Science for studies published from 2000 to March 2026 using search terms for "extreme temperature", "hospitalizations", and "susceptibility". Previous literature investigated the role of demographic, health and social, and environmental indicators as potential drivers of effect heterogeneity in heat-related hospitalizations. However most research focused on few effect modifiers analyzed separately, mainly driven by constraints of existing methods. To date, no study used data-driven approaches to account for the joint, intersectional structure of most indicators. Added value of this studyThis study drew on a comprehensive list of candidate indicators based on previous literature and a comprehensive enumeration of hospitalizations linked with high-dimensional temperature data and regional characteristics. We modeled these indicators of the demographic, health and social, and environmental domains jointly, rather than separately, using a replicable generalized random forest approach. This allowed us to identify the most important drivers of effect heterogeneity across a country while accounting for the joint, intersectional structure of the candidate indicators. We identified substantial within- and across-district heterogeneity, mainly driven by indicators of the demographic domain, followed by indicators of the environmental, and health and social domains. Implications of all the available evidenceWarning systems and adaptation measures for heat are frequently designed around generic categories of vulnerable groups or around a single dominant risk factor, which risks both overlooking places where several moderate disadvantages combine to produce high susceptibility and misdirecting resources toward areas identified by one indicator alone. Therefore, understanding heat susceptibility as the joint, intersectional product of multiple district characteristics instead of single indicators can directly inform heat action plans and heat-health warning systems.

papers.title: Quantifying the global burden of lead exposure from dietary lead intake
papers.abstract: BackgroundLead exposure is estimated to cause approximately 3.5 million premature deaths a year, yet the key ongoing sources of lead exposure are unclear. MethodsWe estimated the contribution of dietary lead intake to global blood lead levels (BLLs) for 7-year-old children and 22-year-old adults by applying the All-Ages Lead Model (AALM) to calculate blood lead levels (BLLs) based on 25 total diet studies (TDS) that quantify dietary lead intake across 46 countries. ResultsFor children, the population-weighted average dietary lead intake in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) (32.0 g/day) was found to be more than three times higher than in high-income countries (HICs) (9.3 g/day), and more than 10 times higher than the FDAs reference level for children (2.2 g/day). The average impact on BLLs for children is estimated to be near 29 g/L in LMICs and near 12 g/L in HICs. Averaged across the TDS data, vegetables (27%) and cereals (24%) were found to contribute the most to dietary lead. ConclusionsWhile there are limitations associated with biokinetic modelling and the TDS data from LMICs, these results suggest that the contribution of dietary lead intake to global lead exposure is in the region of 40 to 50%, suggesting, in turn, that dietary lead intake is likely a major global driver of lead poisoning. Lead absorbed from the environment into food crops is expected to be the key driver of dietary lead. Current regulatory levels for maximum lead concentrations in foods (0.05-0.3 mg/kg) are out-of-date and may imply a dietary lead intake of 200 g/day, far higher than the FDA reference level (2.2 g/day). Collecting representative TDS data in high lead burden countries should be a priority. Further research is also recommended on upstream lead sources and pathways of lead uptake in plants, driving global food contamination. This manuscript is a preprint and has not undergone peer review. It may be revised following review. Highlights- Dietary lead intake is likely a major driver of global lead exposure - Food contamination is largely driven by environmental pollution - International reference levels for lead levels in food are out-of-date - Levels in HICs show interventions to reduce dietary lead intake are possible - Research is needed to aid interventions to reduce lead contamination in food crops

papers.title: The Mental Health of Farm Wives
papers.abstract: ObjectivesResearch on mental health in agriculture has increased in recent years; however, it remains largely focused on farmers themselves and is predominantly male- oriented. The mental health of farm wives and partners, many of whom play integral roles in farm operations, business management, and family life, remains difficult to characterise. This study therefore aims to explore the prevalence and causes of mental health challenges among farm wives and partners, and to investigate their use of, and barriers to, mental health support services. MethodsQuantitative data was collected using over 450 structured questionnaire responses that assessed mental health prevalence, contributing stressors and support service utilisation. ResultsFindings indicate that there is a high prevalence of mental ill health amongst farm wives, seemingly due to industry stressors and support role overwhelm. Interpersonal relationships played a significant role in the types of mental distress experienced and highlighted the toll that farm life can take on farm wives social and emotional connections. Despite a range of formal and informal support services being available, and effective when used, significant barriers to accessing these services were identified, including both practical difficulties and self-stigmatisation due to cultural beliefs. ConclusionsFarm wives and partners experience substantial mental health burdens linked to their diverse and often underrecognized roles within agricultural systems. In future, targeted interventions are needed to reduce stigma, improve service accessibility, and recognize womens contributions within farm enterprises. Further research and dedicated investment are also essential to better understand and help improve the mental health of this overlooked population within agricultural industries.

papers.title: Multi-matrix copper exposure is associated with reduced olfactory bulb volume and odor sensitivity in adolescents
papers.abstract: Copper (Cu) is an essential metal involved in neurobiological processes including energy metabolism and neurotransmission, yet dysregulated Cu levels may adversely affect brain health and olfactory performance. Although olfactory dysfunction has primarily been studied in older adults and neurodegenerative disease, adolescence is a critical period of brain maturation during which the olfactory system may be particularly vulnerable. This cross-sectional study examined associations between Cu exposure, olfactory bulb (OB) volume, and olfactory performance in 200 adolescents and young adults (64% female; ages 13-25) from the Public Health Impact of Metals Exposure cohort. Cu concentrations in blood, urine, hair, and saliva were measured using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging scans estimated left, right, and total OB volumes using a three-stage deep learning pipeline. Olfactory performance was assessed using the Sniffin Sticks test. Weighted quantile sum regression evaluated associations between a Cu mixture index and OB outcomes, while standard linear regression models assessed individual Cu biomarkers. Models were adjusted for age and sex. A higher Cu index was associated with reduced left ({beta} = -0.72, 95% CI [-1.42, -0.02]), right ({beta} = -0.79, 95% CI [-1.43, -0.15]), and total OB volume ({beta} = -1.55, 95% CI [-2.85, -0.25]), as well as lower odor threshold scores ({beta} = -0.23, 95% CI [-0.42, -0.03]). Individual biomarkers were not independently associated with outcomes. These findings suggest that Cu exposure may adversely affect olfactory neurodevelopment during adolescence and highlight the importance of studying environmental exposures relevant to long-term neurological health.

papers.title: Vaccination status and associated factors among healthcare workers providing primary care: a cross-sectional study in Yaounde, Cameroon
papers.abstract: BackgroundHealthcare workers (HCWs) are at increased risk of exposure to vaccine-preventable diseases, including hepatitis B, tuberculosis (TB), and tetanus, due to their occupational environment. Despite the availability of safe and effective vaccines, vaccination coverage among HCWs remains suboptimal in many low- and middle-income countries. This study aimed to determine the vaccination coverage for hepatitis B, tuberculosis, and tetanus among HCWs in district hospitals in Yaounde, Cameroon, and to identify factors associated with incomplete vaccination. MethodsA cross-sectional analytical study was conducted from January to June 2024 across all seven district hospitals in Yaounde. A total of 406 HCWs were enrolled using a structured, self-administered questionnaire. Incomplete vaccination status was defined as nit having received three doses for hepatitis B, at least two doses for TB, and at least three doses for tetanus. Data were analyzed using R Statistics version 4.3.3. Bivariate and multivariate logistic regression models were used to identify predictors of incomplete vaccination, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. ResultsMost of participants were female (75.6%) and aged 30-44 years (65.5%). Full vaccination coverage was 36.2% for hepatitis B, 15.8% for tuberculosis, and 53.4% for tetanus. Unvaccinated proportions were 43.1% for hepatitis B, 0.5% for tuberculosis, and 17.2% for tetanus. Multivariate analysis revealed that HCWs aged 55-66 years were significantly less likely to be incompletely vaccinated against hepatitis B compared to those aged 19-29 years (aOR = 0.07; 95% CI: 0.01-0.39; p = 0.004). Nurses and laboratory technicians were more likely to be incompletely vaccinated than doctors (aOR = 7.06; 95% CI: 3.82-13.6; p < 0.001 and aOR = 3.78; 95% CI: 1.73-8.52; p = 0.001, respectively). Longer professional experience was protective against incomplete vaccination for all three vaccines (p < 0.05). The main barriers to vaccination included high cost, doubts about the need for vaccination, and concerns about side effects. ConclusionsVaccination coverage for hepatitis B, tuberculosis, and tetanus among HCWs in Yaounde remains suboptimal, particularly for hepatitis B. Addressing financial barriers, improving access to vaccines, and implementing targeted educational interventions are essential to enhance vaccine uptake and protect both HCWs and their patients from preventable occupational infections.

papers.title: Strategies to Reach Employees Nurturing Guidance and Trust in Healthcare (STRENGTH): Understanding Employee Drivers for Employer-Based Influenza Vaccination Programs
papers.abstract: BackgroundVaccine hesitancy and logistical barriers continue to limit influenza vaccination uptake among healthcare personnel. The STRENGTH initiative evaluated employee drivers of influenza vaccine acceptance in healthcare workgroups with lower vaccination compliance. MethodsThis mixed-methods program evaluation used a custom Epic electronic medical record dashboard to identify workgroups with lower influenza vaccination rates, followed by focus groups, targeted worksite vaccination clinics, and an anonymous survey. Survey data from 73 respondents were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U tests, Kruskal-Wallis tests, chi-square or Fisher exact tests, and Spearman rank correlations. ResultsRespondents had a mean age of 44.8 years (SD 11.3); 36 of 70 respondents reporting binary gender were male. Convenience of worksite vaccination received the highest importance ratings (mean 4.72/5), followed by protection from influenza (mean 4.38/5). Both were rated significantly above the neutral midpoint of 3 (Wilcoxon p<0.001). The strongest observed Spearman correlations were between peer pressure and leadership participation (rho=0.47) and between protection from influenza and willingness to receive a future combined influenza/COVID-19 vaccine (rho=0.42). ConclusionsConvenience and perceived protection were the most important vaccination drivers. Employer-sponsored workplace vaccination programs can reduce logistical barriers while providing opportunities for targeted education and trust-building.
